extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and legal historians interested in labour, trade, and poor-laws
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Adam Smith's criteria for judging institutions (apprenticeship statutes, corporations, tariffs, poor-laws, parish settlement rules) that shape labour, prices, and the distribution of advantages between town and country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship payment and practical training
rubrics_metrics.description: “A young man would practice with much more diligence and attention, if from the beginning he wrought as a journeyman, being paid in proportion to the little work which he could execute, and paying in his turn for the materials which he might sometimes spoil through awkwardness and inexperience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paid, proportional work during training increases diligence and makes education more effectual and less tedious/expensive. Countervailing effects: masters lose saved apprentice wages over seven years; increased competition may reduce future wages and masters' profits; but the public benefits from cheaper artificers' work. Weigh incentives for skill acquisition against short-term losses to masters and potential long-run wage compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of corporations and corporation laws (to restrain free competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is to prevent this reduction of price, and consequently of wages and profit, by restraining that free competition which would most certainly occasion it, that all corporations, and the greater part of corporation laws have been established.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporations historically serve to limit competition and maintain prices, wages, and profits for insiders. Evaluate corporations by whether they artificially restrain competition and thereby transfer wealth from the broader public (especially country inhabitants) to town-based traders and artificers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town-corporate governance facilitates anti-competitive regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The government of towns-corporate was altogether in the hands of traders and artificers, and it was the manifest interest of every particular class of them, to prevent the market from being overstocked... Each class was eager to establish regulations proper for this purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local governance by insiders tends to produce regulations that limit entry and competition (e.g., restricting apprentices, monopolising local markets). When assessing local regulations, consider who governs and whose interests regulations serve (private class advantage vs public interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations that increase wages/profits shift advantages between town and country
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whatever regulations, therefore, tend to increase those wages and profits beyond what they otherwise would be, tend to enable the town to purchase, with a smaller quantity of its labour, the produce of a greater quantity of the labour of the country. They give the traders and artificers in the town an advantage over the landlords, farmers, and labourers, in the country, and break down that natural equality...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies raising urban wages/profits (via guild rules, tariffs, privileges) should be evaluated for their redistributive effects: they enable towns to command more of country produce and create inequality between urban and rural sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective duties and restrictions on foreign merchants support town monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: “The high duties upon foreign manufactures, and upon all goods imported by alien merchants, all tend to the same purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tariffs and restrictions on foreign merchants operate like corporation protections by insulating towns from external competition. Assess such measures for their role in preserving higher local prices and limiting consumer benefits from foreign competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation spirit and informal combinations (jealousy of strangers, aversion to apprentices)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The corporation-spirit, the jealousy of strangers, the aversion to take apprentices, or to communicate the secret of their trade, generally prevail... and often teach them, by voluntary associations and agreements, to prevent that free competition which they cannot prohibit by bye-laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond formal charters, social norms and voluntary associations can produce anti-competitive outcomes. Policy evaluation must account for both legal rules and prevailing social practices that limit entry or knowledge diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-number trades are prone to combinations that restrict apprentices and labour supply
rubrics_metrics.description: “Half-a-dozen wool-combers, perhaps, are necessary to keep a thousand spinners and weavers at work. By combining not to take apprentices, they can not only engross the employment, but reduce the whole manufacture into a sort of slavery to themselves, and raise the price of their labour much above what is due to the nature of their work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industries with few specialised providers can cartelise entry (e.g., by refusing apprentices) and extract supra‑competitive rents. Regulatory attention should be higher where small provider counts create high risks of collusion and supply restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rural occupations often require diverse judgement and skill (less suited to simple apprenticeship rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not only the art of the farmer... many inferior branches of country labour require much more skill and experience than the greater part of mechanic trades... The man who ploughs the ground... works with instruments of which the health, strength, and temper, are very different upon different occasions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that impose standardised apprenticeship/legal qualifications designed for mechanical trades may be inappropriate for agriculture and other variable rural tasks. Evaluate whether occupational regulation fits the real skill structure of the trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer discipline is the true corrective of workmanship; exclusive corporations weaken it
rubrics_metrics.description: “The real and effectual discipline which is exercised over a workman, is not that of his corporation, but that of his customers... An exclusive corporation necessarily weakens the force of this discipline.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing institutions affecting quality, prioritise mechanisms that maintain consumer choice and reputation. Exclusive privileges that guarantee employment irrespective of quality reduce incentives to maintain standards. Look for evidence of reduced workmanship within monopoly/privilege jurisdictions (e.g., worse work in incorporated towns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations that facilitate trade assemblies or registers promote combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: “A regulation which obliges all those of the same trade in a particular town to enter their names and places of abode in a public register, facilitates such assemblies... A regulation which enables those of the same trade to tax themselves... renders such assemblies necessary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative rules (public registers, permitted self-taxation for mutual aid) that connect members and create common interests can unintentionally facilitate collusion and majority rule against outsiders. Scrutinise procedural provisions that ease coordinated action among traders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporations make majority decisions binding and thus more effective at limiting competition
rubrics_metrics.description: “An incorporation not only renders them necessary, but makes the act of the majority binding upon the whole. ... The majority of a corporation can enact a bye-law, with proper penalties, which will limit the competition more effectually and more durably than any voluntary combination whatever.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate corporate governance structures for internal majoritarian powers that can impose binding restrictions (bye-laws, penalties) on members; such powers magnify anti‑competitive potential compared with voluntary associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction of labour and capital mobility by apprenticeship statutes and exclusive privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: “The statute of apprenticeship obstructs the free circulation of labour from one employment to another... The exclusive privileges of corporations obstruct it from one place to another, even in the same employment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether legal constraints (apprenticeship rules, residency/settlement rules, corporate privileges) prevent workers and capital from reallocating to more productive or growing employments/locations, which can cause mismatches and persistent regional/sectoral disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectoral mismatch example: overlapping skills should enable labour mobility absent legal barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: “The arts of weaving plain linen and plain silk... are almost entirely the same... If any of those three capital manufactures, therefore, were decaying, the workmen might find a resource in one of the other two which was in a more prosperous condition; and their wages would neither rise too high in the thriving, nor sink too low in the decaying manufacture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating apprenticeship and entry restrictions, consider technical similarity across trades: where skill overlap is high, legal barriers unnecessarily prevent reallocation and exacerbate unemployment in declining industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parish settlement rules obstruct free circulation of common labour (poor-laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of statutes: forty days undisturbed residence to gain settlement (13–14 Charles II); notice requirements added (1 James II); publication in church after notice (3 William III); four alternative ways to gain settlement without notice: being taxed to parish rates, elected to parish office for a year, serving an apprenticeship in the parish, or being hired into service there for a year and continuing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement law mechanisms (residence periods, notice, publication, and narrow alternative paths) make it difficult for poor people to change parishes and find employment, thereby restricting labour mobility. Evaluate poor-law design for administrative barriers, opportunities for fraud, and impacts on ability of labour to relocate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly funded education for certain professions increases competition and reduces private reward
rubrics_metrics.description: “It has been considered as of so much importance that a proper number of young people should be educated for certain professions, that sometimes the public... have established many pensions, scholarships... which draw many more people into those trades than could otherwise pretend to follow them... the competition of the poor takes away the reward of the rich.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free or publicly-funded professional education can oversupply particular careers (clergy, law, physic), depressing private returns and potentially degrading the professions if education becomes universally subsidised. Policy assessment should weigh public benefits of accessible education against risks of overcrowding particular occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological and institutional change (printing) can expand supply and reduce rewards in literary professions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Before the invention of the art of printing... the only employment by which a man of letters could make any thing by his talents... The time and study... required to qualify an eminent teacher... But the usual reward of the eminent teacher bears no proportion to that of the lawyer or physician, because the trade of the one is crowded with indigent people, who have been brought up to it at the public expense... Before the invention of the art of printing, a scholar and a beggar seem to have been terms very nearly synonymous.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for how innovation (printing) and market expansion change labour supply in cultural/intellectual fields. Assess regulation and public support in light of technological shifts that alter returns to different kinds of intellectual labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal attempts to fix wages are typically ineffective and can have unintended direction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whenever the law has attempted to regulate the wages of workmen, it has always been rather to lower them than to raise them. But the law has, upon many occasions, attempted to raise the wages of curates... In both cases, the law seems to have been equally ineffectual... because it has never been able to hinder either the one from being willing to accept of less than the legal allowance... or the other from receiving more...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wage-fixing statutes often fail because they ignore market forces and individual incentives; workers may accept below‑legal pay due to necessity, and employers may pay above legal minima due to competition for labour. Evaluate wage regulation by its enforceability and interaction with labour supply/demand.
